hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Calling metformin a mitochondrial poison sounds dramatic, but it's an accurate description of how the most prescribed diabetes drug in the world actually lowers blood glucose. Unfortunately, the mechanism is a kind of blunt instrument.

One of metformin's best-described actions is that it inhibits complex I of the mitochondrial electron transport chain, the first step cells use to turn the fuel we eat into ATP. With complex I partly blocked, the cell makes less energy, and that energy shortfall activates AMPK and slows how much glucose the liver makes and releases into the blood. Put plainly, metformin lowers glucose largely by making cells a little worse at producing energy, and the liver and gut wall take the heaviest exposure because they pull the drug in through their transporters.

That matters most in muscle when someone is trying to get healthier through exercise, since the main benefits of training come from muscle building more and better mitochondria and becoming more sensitive to insulin.

In older adults doing 12 weeks of aerobic training, the group taking metformin lost much of the gain in mitochondrial respiration that exercise produced, and the improvement in whole-body insulin sensitivity was blunted compared with the group on placebo.

In another trial of older adults doing 14 weeks of resistance training, the people taking metformin gained less muscle mass and less thigh muscle than those taking placebo, and the usual training response in their muscle tissue was dampened.

I'm not overtly opposed to metformin, and for a sedentary person with high blood glucose it can have a place, but I see its usefulness dropping as exercise goes up, since the more someone trains, the more the drug works against the very adaptations they're working for.

I also find it bizarre that metformin gets promoted as a longevity hack, because it's hard for me to believe that a drug that compromises mitochondrial function, which is so central to healthy aging, would be the key to living longer.

For anyone using exercise to improve their metabolic health, and especially for older adults trying to hold on to muscle, it's worth knowing that metformin and exercise can pull in opposite directions inside the muscle cell.
hits.draft_en:
Prof Ben Bikman makes a point every older bloke on metformin should hear.

Metformin lowers blood sugar partly by making cells a bit worse at making energy. In older adults doing 12 weeks of aerobic training, the ones on metformin lost much of the gain in their muscle's energy output that exercise gave the placebo group. In a 14-week weights trial, the metformin group put on less muscle.

He's not saying stop it. If you're on it and you're training to hold on to your muscle, have a yarn with your doctor about it. Don't change any medication on your own.

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
I get asked a lot about magnesium supplements. Here are my general thoughts.

Start with magnesium-rich foods - leafy greens, nuts, seeds, and legumes. Supplements can help when your diet falls short.

Citrate, glycinate/bisglycinate, and chloride are good options. Citrate and chloride are generally better absorbed than oxide. Malate and taurate are alternatives. There isn’t one clear winner for everyone.

For sleep, I take magnesium glycinate/bisglycinate a couple of hours before bed. It’s my preference, although it hasn’t been established as the best form for sleep. L-threonate also has some interesting, early research for sleep and cognition.

Some other considerations to keep in mind:

• Look for elemental magnesium on the label.

• The adult upper limit is 350 mg/day from supplements and magnesium-containing medications (excluding food). That limit primarily reflects gastrointestinal side effects. Smaller doses throughout the day may improve absorption and be easier on your stomach.

• Athletes and frequent sauna users may need slightly more, because magnesium is lost through sweat.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Rhonda Patrick gets asked about magnesium a lot. Her short version:

Start with food: leafy greens, nuts, seeds and legumes. Supplements are for when your diet falls short.

Citrate, glycinate and chloride are decent options and absorb better than oxide. There's no one clear winner for everyone. Check the label for "elemental" magnesium, and keep supplements under 350 mg a day, because more than that is mostly a gut problem.

She also says people who sweat a lot can lose more of it. Plenty of us on the tools sweat all day in summer, so it's worth getting the food side right first.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Calories matter, but when it comes to hunger and satiety, not all calories are equal. A meal built mostly on carbohydrate does a weaker job of switching on the body's fullness signals than a meal built on protein or fat, even when the calories are exactly the same, and the gap is widest in people who are already insulin resistant.

One study gave people three different meals on separate days, each with the same calories but with most of the energy coming from carbohydrate, protein or fat, and then tracked the gut hormones that tell the brain whether a person has eaten enough over the next six hours. Some of the subjects were lean and insulin sensitive, while others had obesity and insulin resistance. All of them still had normal blood glucose.

GLP-1 (a satiety signal) rose more after the protein meal and the fat meal than after the carbohydrate meal, and that was true in both the lean and overweight people. In the those with insulin resistance, the fat meal also produced a bigger rise in PYY, another hormone that signals fullness, and the protein and fat meals pushed ghrelin, the main hunger hormone, down further than the carbohydrate meal did.

This helps explain why a breakfast based on carbs so often leaves a person hungry again by mid-morning, while a breakfast of eggs and meat can hold them until lunch. The body's own satiety system responds more strongly to protein and fat, and a person who is insulin resistant appears to get even less of that signal from a carb-heavy meal, which makes it harder for them to stop eating at the very point when they most need to.

If someone struggles with hunger soon after eating, it's clear that building meals around protein and fat rather than carbohydrate gives the body's natural fullness hormones a much better chance to do their job.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Insulin resistance can begin within days of overeating, and the first warning sign is a rise in insulin, well before blood glucose or the scale gives anything away.

Healthy men with normal metabolism were fed a large surplus of a typical American diet, about half of it carbohydrate, for a single week. Their blood was checked every morning after an overnight fast, and their fasting glucose never budged, which by the usual standards would mean their metabolism was perfectly fine.

Their insulin told a very different story. Fasting insulin rose by the second day and kept climbing every day after that, ending the week about two and a half times higher than where it started, and by then the men's bodies were taking up only about half as much glucose in response to insulin as they had at the beginning.

This is the pattern I see over and over, where a steady flood of food, much of it carbohydrate, pushes insulin up and keeps it up, and the cells respond by turning down their sensitivity to it, so that chronically high insulin is driving the very insulin resistance it later gets blamed on.

It also shows why fasting glucose is such a poor early test, since these men would have passed a routine checkup at the very moment their insulin was climbing and their cells were becoming resistant to it.

If someone wants to protect their insulin sensitivity, it's clear that keeping insulin from running high, by not overeating, and particularly not overeating carbohydrate, matters well before blood glucose or body weight shows any change.

“Plop, plop, fizz, fizz—oh, what a relief it is.” 
Alka-Seltzer offered quick, temporary relief for heartburn, but it never fixed the underlying problem. Meanwhile, GERD has become far more common.

Global data show prevalent cases rising from about 451 million in 1990 to roughly 826 million in 2021—an increase of around 83%. Incident cases climbed about 80% over the same period. In Western countries, weekly heartburn or regurgitation symptoms often affect 18–28% of adults. 

The rise accelerated after the mid-1990s, tracking the obesity epidemic and the spread of Western dietary patterns. Esophageal adenocarcinoma rates also climbed sharply in the US over recent decades.

The main drivers are clear. Obesity and central adiposity raise intra-abdominal pressure, increase transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations, and promote hiatal hernia. There is a dose-response relationship with BMI; weight gain worsens symptoms, while weight loss improves them. 

Diet plays a major role too: high intakes of refined carbohydrates, sugars, and ultra-processed foods, along with common triggers such as caffeine, chocolate, fried foods, acidic items, alcohol, and carbonated drinks. Late or large evening meals and sedentary habits add further pressure.

Very-low-carbohydrate and ketogenic approaches have solid evidence for improving GERD, and a carnivore diet represents the most extreme version—essentially zero plant carbohydrates and fermentable fibers. In a 2006 study of obese patients with GERD who ate under 20 grams of carbohydrate per day, distal esophageal acid exposure fell from 5.1% to 2.5% and the Johnson-DeMeester score dropped from 34.7 to 14.0 within about six days, with clear symptom improvement—before major weight loss could explain the change. 

Meta-analyses confirm that low-carbohydrate diets reduce esophageal acid exposure time by roughly 2.8% on average.
Likely mechanisms include elimination of fermentable carbohydrates (reducing gas, distension, and sphincter relaxations), lower gastric volume, substantial weight loss that eases abdominal pressure, and removal of common dietary triggers. Many people on carnivore report rapid resolution of long-standing GERD and the ability to stop acid-suppressing drugs. While large trials of pure carnivore are still lacking, the low-carb data, mechanistic logic, and consistent real-world reports make it a rational dietary intervention for many.

Individual responses vary, and anyone with Barrett’s esophagus, erosive disease, or alarm symptoms needs medical follow-up. Antacids and PPIs mask symptoms; addressing excess carbohydrates, excess weight, and the modern dietary pattern offers a more direct path for a large share of those affected.

Four in ten young American adults without diabetes are already insulin resistant, and nearly half of them aren't obese.

That finding comes from national health survey data on adults between 18 and 44 who had neither diabetes nor heart disease, which is the group most people assume is metabolically safe. Insulin resistance was common across a full decade of surveys, and the share stayed high from one survey cycle to the next.

The young adults with insulin resistance were already carrying more of the problems that eventually lead to heart disease and diabetes, with high blood pressure and high cholesterol each about twice as common as in their insulin-sensitive peers, along with lower levels of physical activity.

The part that matters most for how people get screened is that body weight only partly lined up with insulin resistance. A higher BMI, a larger waist and more body fat were all associated with it, but nearly half of the young adults who were insulin resistant weren't obese, which means a normal reading on the bathroom scale doesn't rule it out.

Insulin resistance also tends to hide on standard blood work. Glucose can stay normal for years because the pancreas keeps making more insulin to hold it there, so the earliest sign of trouble is often a rising fasting insulin, and that's a test most doctors don't routinely order.

For a young adult, this is the stretch of life when insulin resistance is easiest to turn around, long before glucose climbs high enough to earn a diagnosis of prediabetes or diabetes, and the researchers themselves concluded that screening for insulin resistance regardless of BMI may be needed.

If a young adult wants to know where they stand metabolically, adding a fasting insulin test to the usual glucose check gives a far clearer picture than weight or glucose alone.

hits.text:
Van Ness rotationplasty: the surgery that turns your foot into a knee
One of the strangest-looking procedures in orthopedics is the Van Ness (or Van Nes / Borggreve) rotationplasty. 
It’s mainly used for bone cancers like osteosarcoma near the knee in kids, or severe congenital limb deficiencies. Instead of a high above-knee amputation, surgeons remove the tumor and the knee joint, then rotate the lower leg 180 degrees and reattach it so the ankle sits where the knee used to be. The foot ends up pointing backward. 
The nerves and blood vessels stay connected. Once it heals, the patient gets a custom prosthesis that the backward-facing foot and ankle slip into. Pointing the foot straightens the prosthetic “knee”; flexing the ankle bends it. You end up with a living, muscle-powered knee joint instead of a passive mechanical one. 
It looks bizarre (and the cosmetic appearance is the biggest downside), but functionally it often beats a standard above-knee amputation: better control, lower energy cost for walking, more durability, and the ability to run, jump, and play sports. Because it’s the patient’s own tissue, it also grows with a child. 
First done in the 1920s–1930s for tuberculosis, popularized by Dutch surgeon Cornelis van Nes in the 1950s, and refined for tumors in the decades since. Still uncommon, still visually wild, and still one of the better functional options when the alternative is losing the knee entirely. 
Weird? Yes. Effective? For the right patient, absolutely.

FALLBACK FOODS ARE NOT HEALTH FOODS.

Fallback foods are what you eat when you can't get what you really need. The goal of fallback foods is to prevent true starvation, to to improve your health. Primatologists define them as "resources of relatively low preference" eaten "when preferred foods are unavailable." The word preferred here refers to best-choice-for-health, not just for taste.

Optimization foods are what people chased first. For hunter-gatherers, that always meant animals.

The Hadza of Tanzania still hunt and forage. Asked to rank their 5 main foods, they put meat second, behind only honey. Tubers came in dead last. The researchers wrote that tubers "fit the definition of fallback foods." Women of childbearing age had more body fat in camps that brought in more meat, and less where more tubers came in.

Worldwide, 73% of hunter-gatherer societies got more than half their food from animals. Only 14% got more than half from plants.

Then came farming, and grain became the daily staple. In 19 of 21 societies that made the switch, the skeletons show health got worse. They had more cavities, infections and nutritional deficiencies. In most studies, people got shorter.

In the poor South, cornmeal was the main source of calories. At its peak, pellagra caused at least 250,000 cases and 7,000 deaths a year. In 1915 Goldberger fed prison volunteers biscuits, gravy, cornbread, grits, rice, syrup, collards and yams. 6 of 11 came down with pellagra. Orphans he gave fresh meat and plenty of milk got better.

Nutrition "experts" who haven't studied anthropology don't know that these food experiments have already been tried, over and over, by different societies. The same result keeps showing up. Meat, eggs, organs and fish were the optimization foods, often reserved for royalty and the rich. Tubers, grains and corn were poverty foods, handed to the masses, to slaves and to prisoners. In medieval England, the king reserved the hunting of deer and wild boar for himself. At Cahokia, the high-status people ate much more animal protein, and the low-status people ate more maize. Enslaved people in the American South were commonly issued a peck of cornmeal a week, plus a little pork or fish.

Fallback foods kept people alive when there was nothing better. In 1992 the USDA put grains at the base of the food pyramid anyway. 6 to 11 servings a day.

outsiders.text:
What happens when you put Gemini 4 Carbon to work in the lab? 🔬

Researchers are using our latest model in Google @Antigravity to tackle multi-step problems across physics, math, and the life sciences. https://t.co/pe1QLnFxh8

outsiders.name: Ethan Mollick
outsiders.text: I think contrary to many of our expectations, we have not seen a Fable class open model more than 8 months after Fable/Mythos was first made public. https://t.co/7swxpxMpyv

outsiders.name: Aravind Srinivas
outsiders.text: Teammate on Fable 5.2 built an open-world driving game set in a neon 1986 Miami that runs in your browser at https://t.co/Ckl50J4MS1. No game engine, no Three.js and no external assets: Teammate wrote its own WebGL2 renderer, and the city, cars, garage, rain and engine sounds are https://t.co/fDiCuVNJ7i

outsiders.name: Aravind Srinivas
outsiders.text: Teammates are awesome, and you can build them with any frontier model of your choice on Perplexity. No other product lets you do this. https://t.co/d5sNFVXVAt

outsiders.name: Aravind Srinivas
outsiders.text: A week later, it’s 11x more agent hours per week from Teammate. Growing more than 50% week over week (was 7x last week). The number of employees getting an extra workday (8+ hours) and extra work week (40+ hours) from Teammate has more than tripled in a week since September. https://t.co/nAPbK4OGUO https://t.co/xMVB6hoPHq

outsiders.name: clem 🤗
outsiders.text:
Too many people treat AI as a zero-sum race. Open-source is winning by doing the opposite: collaboration over competition! 

This is why we’re excited to release today the first part of our partnership with @OpenRouter to make open models easier to use for all! Hugging Face for storage and collaboration. OpenRouter for inference. Connected so you can:

🤗 Run OpenRouter inference directly on Hugging Face
🔓 Access Open model weights directly from OpenRouter
🤖 Store your OpenRouter agent traces on HF to inspect them, train better models or share them with the world!

More collaboration. Fewer zero-sum games. More power to AI builders. Let’s build! 💛💛💛

outsiders.name: Aravind Srinivas
outsiders.text: Perplexity agents (Computer or Teammate) can cite each number in a financial research and analysis task to the exact line item on the filings  https://t.co/f4SziblIoc

outsiders.name: Aravind Srinivas
outsiders.text: Slack is awesome and all Perplexity products are built and dogfooded with Slackbots. Perplexity has the best  Slack agent (Computer) in the industry right now, and we will be migrating that to a persistent Teammate that you can assign any task to. https://t.co/NJn0fpEcJR

outsiders.name: Aravind Srinivas
outsiders.text: Announcing Perplexity Monitor: an API that lets you track any event or topic or changes to webpages and set up webhooks to update you. Costs a $1 for 1000 runs. https://t.co/h5kCVvxeW0

The score counts only NEW originals, not repeats still climbing from yesterday. New hits >=5k per day: median 28, top quarter 36+, best 45. New views per day: median ~0.95M, top fifth 2.0M+, best 2.7M. Score = half new hits vs 36, half new views vs 2.0M, each capped at 100%. Day Target is DONE only when both are met.
